**Evidence basis:** This summary uses the video's English auto-generated captions. Financial figures, governance arrangements, and filing disclosures below are the presenter's account, not an independent review of the prospectus. He says the analysis is incomplete, the IPO valuation is not yet known, and the video is not an investment recommendation. [00:00–02:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=0s)

### Main takeaways

- **Owning shares does not necessarily give investors control.** The presenter describes a trust empowered to elect a board majority and a founder-controlled share carrying 50.1% of shareholder voting power. These arrangements limit public shareholders' influence over management and Anthropic's public-benefit mission. He also describes share grants to a philanthropic fund that can dilute other shareholders: issuing additional shares reduces existing holders' percentage ownership. [03:10–06:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=190s)
- **Cloud partners are also suppliers, investors, and competitors.** He reports that roughly 80% of revenue comes from usage-based charges rather than subscriptions. Separately, cloud-provider distribution accounts for 48% of revenue, up from 11% in 2023: Amazon, Google, and Microsoft sell Anthropic's services to their customers and split the fees. Those overlapping roles create potential conflicts, though the video does not establish that any partner will withdraw. [06:11–07:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=371s)
- **Some financing will be settled in shares rather than cash.** The video reports $108.6 billion in convertible notes and $157.5 billion in convertible preferred stock: financing instruments set to become company shares before the initial public offering (IPO). Issuing those shares dilutes existing holders. [05:17–06:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=317s) The presenter cautions against treating both amounts as ordinary debt to be repaid in cash. He says most of their value will instead move into shareholder equity when they convert. He also notes that research spending can create valuable models without creating a corresponding asset on the balance sheet. [07:14–09:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=434s)
- **Adjusted profits leave out costs borne by shareholders.** He contrasts a reported adjusted operating margin of 10% with a −4.3% margin under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) for the first half of 2026. The adjusted measure excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions that the standard accounting measure includes. His point is that paying through share issuance still costs investors ownership, even if it avoids a cash payment. He also notes that the second quarter turned operationally profitable; that is different from reporting an overall net profit. [09:20–11:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=560s)
- **A higher valuation can produce a larger accounting loss.** In the presenter's explanation, rising company value increases the recorded value of the convertible instruments. These “fair-value” increases are non-cash charges that reduce reported net income, rather than immediate cash payments; adjusted net income excludes them. Conversion before the IPO would remove the existing instruments, but would not guarantee profitability. He cites further upfront infrastructure expenses and plans for short-term compute agreements that cost more than longer-term arrangements. [09:20–10:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=560s), [11:28–13:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=688s)
- **Future payments still need funding.** The presenter cites $265.6 billion in purchase commitments, $371.6 billion in payments over the lives of upcoming leases, and $161.2 billion for an upcoming finance lease excluding interest. These are categories with different terms, not a combined bill due today. His concern is that long-lived, largely non-cancellable commitments could leave Anthropic unable to find cash for payments when due if revenue growth slows or access to new capital dries up. [12:17–15:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=737s)
- **Fast growth does not settle what the shares are worth.** He describes potential selling pressure when existing investors become eligible to sell their shares, while noting that the schedule and final IPO valuation are not yet available. His example of a valuation roughly 100 times annual revenue depends on a rumored $2 trillion valuation, not a confirmed offering price. Sustained growth could support returns, but he says the company itself expects the exceptional early-adoption growth rate to slow. [15:26–17:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o&t=926s)

### Why it matters for AI economics

Editorial interpretation: strong demand for an AI product does not by itself show that its provider can fund future compute commitments without reducing existing shareholders' ownership. The video explains why those questions need separate examination; it does not establish that Anthropic will succeed or fail, or that its shares are attractively priced.

Full video: [The Plain Bagel — The Numbers Behind Anthropic](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZrgRjdJs3o).
